query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding alloying elements such as Hf to refractory high-entropy alloys can improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability by enhancing phase stability and dislocation movement.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys in a single-phase BCC structure
generation.intervention: Adding Hf as an alloying element to the refractory high-entropy alloy composition
generation.mechanism: The addition of Hf enhances phase stability by reducing the valence electron concentration (VEC) value, which in turn improves dislocation movement and thus mechanical performance under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in mechanical performance of at least 15% in terms of yield strength compared to the baseline alloy without Hf addition
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloys without Hf addition
generation.boundary: The improvement in mechanical performance is expected to occur within the range of 0-1000°C and under irradiation doses up to 10 dpa
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Hf to be added and the resulting microstructure may affect the outcome, and further research is needed to determine the optimal composition and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare refractory high-entropy alloy samples with and without Hf addition, and subject them to high-temperature and irradiation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yield strength of the alloy with Hf addition is not at least 15% higher than that of the baseline alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

The strategy then consists in finding a combination of elements that can lower the VEC value. It is worth emphasizing that a VEC value of 4.4 is based on a few works on HEAs and therefore is not considered as an absolute number. Group IV elements can then be used to pursue this approach (e.g., Ti, Zr, and Hf) and modify the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA. In the process of pursuing high-performance materials, the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [] were introduced. The preeminent properties (such as high strength [,], good corrosion resistance [,,], fine tribological properties [,], remarkable softening resistance [,], and outstanding irradiation tolerance [,,,], etc.) enhance the application competitiveness of HEAs under extreme environments. Among them, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], which are characterized by a high melting point and prepared by methods such as vacuum arc melting, suspension melting, spark plasma sintering [], and wire electric discharge machining [], are expected to play a role in future high-temperature applications []. Compared with conventional alloys, HEAs, especially the body-centered cubic (BCC) structured ones composed of refractory elements, exhibit better irradiation tolerance for the extreme lattice distortions and chemical complexity, such as prominent resistance to hardening [,], suppressed dislocation evolution [,,], low volume swelling rate [,], and reduced radiation-induced segregation [,,], etc. Hence, the HEAs are considered to be a promising candidate for nuclear structural materials [,]

Especially in high-temperature applications, the microstructure of EHEA, with FCC+BCC phases, exhibits characteristics that are similar to the γ′ phase of nickel-based alloys, which has demonstrated outstanding resistance to oxidation [,]. Moreover, the unique eutectic solidification structure of EHEA provides a lower phase interface energy, and the significant sluggish diffusion effects characteristic of high-entropy alloys show its superior stability at higher temperatures [,]. Therefore, EHEA has great potential as a high-temperature protective coating. On the other hand, exploration of the properties of alloying elements and rare earth elements for high-entropy alloys has also never stopped [,,,]. Research about the effect of alloying elements on the performance of HEAs has predominantly concentrated on the mechanical properties while the literature indicates that conventional and high-entropy alloys and Y and Hf co-doping can effectively enhance the high-temperature oxidation resistance of alloys [,,].
